'''''Artemisia scoparia''''' (Waldst. & Kit., 1802), commonly known as '''virgate wormwood''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |location=Pocheon |pages=360–361 |access-date=25 January 2017 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |archive-date=25 May 2017}}</ref> '''capillary wormwood''',<ref name=":0" /> or '''redstem wormwood''', is a perennial aromatic herb in the genus ''[[Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]'', in the [[Asteraceae|sunflower family]]. It is widespread across much of [[Eurasia]] from [[France]] to [[Japan]], including [[China]], [[India]], [[Russia]], [[Germany]], [[Poland]], and central and southwest Asia.<ref name="florachina">{{cite web |title=Flora of China: ''Artemisia scoparia'' Waldstein & Kitaibel |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200023326 |access-date=2024-01-01}}</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=artemisia+scoparia Altervista Flora Italiana, Assenzio scopario, ''Artemisia scoparia'' Waldst. & Kit.] includes photos and European distribution map</ref> In [[Mandarin Chinese]] it is known as '''yīn chén''' ({{lang|zh|茵陳}}; also romanised ''Yin Chen'') or '''zhū máo hāo''' ({{lang|zh|猪毛蒿}}). The dried herb — ''Artemisiae Scopariae Herba'' (ASH) — is an officially recognised drug in the [[Chinese Pharmacopoeia]] and is considered interchangeable with the closely related ''[[Artemisia capillaris]]'' Thunb. for medicinal purposes.<ref name="ding2021">{{cite journal |last1=Ding |first1=Jiwei |last2=Wang |first2=Linlin |last3=He |first3=Chunnian |last4=Zhao |first4=Jun |last5=Si |first5=Lijun |last6=Huang |first6=Hua |date=2021-06-12 |title=Artemisia scoparia: Traditional uses, active constituents and pharmacological effects |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874121001860 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=273 |article-number=113960 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2021.113960 |pmid=33636317 |s2cid=232065726 |issn=0378-8741 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Its pollen can be allergenic in sensitised individuals.<ref name="jaggi1987">{{cite journal |last1=Jaggi |first1=K.S. |last2=Gangal |first2=S.V. |year=1987 |title=Isolation and identification of pollen allergens of ''Artemisia scoparia'' |journal=[[J Allergy Clin Immunol]] |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=569–572 |doi=10.1016/0091-6749(87)90008-X |pmid=3668120}}</ref>
 
== Botanical description ==
 
According to the [[Flora of China]], ''A. scoparia'' is a perennial and aromatic herb 45–100 cm high, though it can sometimes reach 130 cm. The stem is often basally lignified with a purple tinge and heavily branched from the lower portion. Young stem branches and leaves are sea-green, covered with white or greyish silky hairs (sericeous); at maturity they become yellowish and glabrous. The basal leaf petiole is 2–3 cm long; the leaf blade is elliptic to ovate-oblong, 1.5–5 cm long, and 2–3-pinnatisect with segments in 3–4 pairs. The plant is strongly aromatic, particularly in the young spring growth that is traditionally harvested for medicinal use before the stem elongates.<ref name="ding2021"/><ref name="temperate">{{cite web |last=Fern |first=Ken |title=Artemisia scoparia |publisher=Useful Temperate Plants Database |url=https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Artemisia+scoparia |access-date=2024-06-03}}</ref>
 
== Ecology ==
 
=== Habitat ===
 
''A. scoparia'' grows in a wide variety of disturbed and open habitats. In Japan it is associated with waste ground; across China it colonises slopes, forest margins, roadsides, steppe, terraces, desert margins, and dry river beds, from low elevations up to 3,200 metres.<ref name="temperate"/> It is drought-tolerant once established and grows best in well-drained, poor, dry soils in a warm, sunny position. Like many ''Artemisia'' species it tends to be longer-lived and more aromatic when grown in impoverished conditions. It is rarely browsed by deer.<ref name="temperate"/>
 
=== Insect herbivores ===
 
''A. scoparia'' produces a rich array of defensive secondary metabolites — including sesquiterpene lactones and aromatic essential oils — that are toxic to many herbivorous insects. Despite this, it is a recorded larval host plant for certain species. The noctuid moth ''[[Schinia scutosa]]'' (the spotted clover moth, family [[Noctuidae]]), which ranges from Europe across Siberia to Japan and the Near East, uses several ''Artemisia'' species as larval foodplants, including ''A. scoparia'', ''[[Artemisia vulgaris|A. vulgaris]]'', ''[[Artemisia campestris|A. campestris]]'', ''[[Artemisia abrotanum|A. abrotanum]]'', and ''[[Artemisia dracunculus|A. dracunculus]]''. More broadly, the genus ''Artemisia'' supports a notable community of specialist [[Lepidoptera]], including multiple species of ''[[Cucullia]]'' (shark moths), ''[[Coleophora]]'' (case-bearer moths), and ''[[Eucosma]]'' (tortrix moths) whose larvae feed on various wormwood species. Specific records for ''A. scoparia'' as a host are limited compared with the more widely studied ''[[Artemisia absinthium|A. absinthium]]'' and ''[[Artemisia vulgaris|A. vulgaris]]''.
 
=== Edible uses ===
 
Young leaves of ''A. scoparia'' are recorded as edible when cooked, though this use is minor and not widely documented.<ref name="temperate"/>
 
== Cultivation ==
 
''A. scoparia'' is not in general commercial cultivation as a garden plant in the United Kingdom or Western Europe, and is not currently listed by the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]. It is described in horticultural references as easily grown in well-drained, circumneutral or slightly alkaline loamy soil in a warm, sunny, dry position. Plants are longer-lived, hardier, and more aromatic in poor dry soils. It can be propagated from seed surface-sown in a greenhouse in spring, pricked out when large enough to handle, and planted out in early summer; alternatively it can be sown in situ in late spring.<ref name="temperate"/> Across its native range it is principally harvested from wild populations for local medicinal use, essential oil extraction, and food use, rather than formally cultivated.
 
== Phytochemistry ==
 
More than 70 chemical components and plant secondary metabolites have been isolated and identified from ''A. scoparia''.<ref name="zhu2020">{{cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Yajun |year=2020 |title=Recent progress in the study of Artemisiae Scopariae Herba (Yin Chen), a promising medicinal herb for liver diseases |journal=Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy |volume=132 |article-number=110679 |doi=10.1016/j.biopha.2020.110679 |pmid=32858498 }}</ref> The principal bioactive compounds include:
 
* '''[[Scoparone]]''' (6,7-dimethoxycoumarin; also known as 6,7-dimethylesculetin) — the major pharmacologically active coumarin constituent<ref name="aschema">{{cite journal |last1=Hoult |first1=J.R.S. |last2=Payá |first2=M. |year=1996 |title=Pharmacological and biochemical actions of simple coumarins: natural products with therapeutic potential |journal=[[Gen. Pharmacol.]] |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=713–722 |pmid=8853310 |doi=10.1016/0306-3623(95)02112-4}}</ref>
* '''[[Capillarisin]]''' — a chromone with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties<ref name="ccas">{{cite web |title=Chemical Study on Artemisia scoparia |url=http://www.wanfangdata.com.cn/qikan/periodical.Articles/zgyaokdxxb/zgya2004/0405/040504.htm |access-date=November 17, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930165414/http://www.wanfangdata.com.cn/qikan/periodical.Articles/zgyaokdxxb/zgya2004/0405/040504.htm |archive-date=September 30, 2007}}</ref>
* '''[[Chlorogenic acid]]''' and its butyl ester — polyphenolic acids with antioxidant activity
* '''[[Scopoletin]]''' and '''7-methylesculetin''' — coumarin derivatives
* '''[[7-Methoxycoumarin]]''' (herniarin)
* '''[[Beta-Sitosterol|β-Sitosterol]]''' — a phytosterol
* '''Capillin''' — a polyacetylenic compound
* '''Isosabandin''', '''[[Sabandin A]]''' and '''[[Sabandin B]]''' — furanocoumarins<ref name="sbdina">{{cite journal |last1=Ali |first1=M.S. |last2=Jahangir |first2=M. |last3=Saleem |first3=M. |year=2003 |title=Structural distinction between sabandins A and B from ''Artemisia scoparia'' waldst. (Asteraceae) |journal=[[Nat. Prod. Res.]] |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=1–4 |pmid=12674134 |doi=10.1080/10575630290020640 |s2cid=32672104}}</ref>
* '''Magnolioside''' (isoscopoletin-β-<small>D</small>-glucopyranoside)
* Flavonoids including isorhamnetin and quercetin derivatives
 
The relative abundance of these constituents varies significantly with the harvest season. The bioactive compound profiles shift considerably across growing stages, which is consistent with the traditional preference for young spring plant material.<ref name="ding2021"/><ref name="zhu2020"/>
 
== Essential oil ==
 
The seeds and flowering stems of ''A. scoparia'' yield approximately 0.75% essential oil on distillation.<ref name="temperate"/> Studies of oils from plants collected at different altitudes and across different regions have found that the major constituents include [[capillene]] (9.6–31.8%), [[methyleugenol]] (0.2–26.6%), [[beta-myrcene|β-myrcene]] (1.9–21.4%), [[gamma-terpinene|γ-terpinene]] (1.5–19.4%), [[trans-β-caryophyllene]] (0.8–12.4%), [[β-Pinene]] (8–19%), [[capillin]], [[limonene]], and [[eugenol]]. The precise profile varies significantly with altitude and harvest conditions.<ref name="eoaltitude">{{cite journal |last1=Parveen |first1=A. |last2=Abbas |first2=M. G. |last3=Keefover-Ring |first3=K. |last4=Binyameen |first4=M. |last5=Mozūraitis |first5=R. |last6=Azeem |first6=M. |year=2024 |title=Chemical Composition of Essential Oils from Natural Populations of ''Artemisia scoparia'' Collected at Different Altitudes: Antibacterial, Mosquito Repellent, and Larvicidal Effects |journal=Molecules |volume=29 |issue=6 |doi=10.3390/molecules29061352 |doi-access=free |pmid=38542997 |pmc=10975050}}</ref>
 
The essential oil has been demonstrated in laboratory studies to have significant repellent and fumigant activity against stored-product insect pests. Studies have shown repellent and toxic effects against the pulse beetle ''[[Callosobruchus maculatus]]'', the rice weevil ''[[Sitophilus oryzae]]'', and the red flour beetle ''[[Tribolium castaneum]]''. One study found that a concentration of 37 μL per litre of air with an exposure time of 24 hours was sufficient to achieve 100% kill of the tested insects.<ref name="negahban2006">{{cite journal |last1=Negahban |first1=M. |year=2006 |title=Efficacy of essential oil from ''Artemisia scoparia'' Waldst. & Kit. against ''Tribolium castaneum'' (Herbst) (Coleoptera: Tenebrionidae) |journal=Journal of Stored Products Research |doi=10.1016/j.jspr.2005.03.004 |doi-broken-date=3 June 2026 }}</ref> The oil has also shown repellent activity against the yellow fever mosquito ''[[Aedes aegypti]]'': oil from one tested population exhibited 100% repellency for 15 minutes at a concentration of 33.3 μg/cm², a result comparable to [[DEET]] at the same concentration.<ref name="eoaltitude"/> This insect-repellent activity is consistent with the broader pattern seen across the genus ''Artemisia'', whose aromatic essential oils have long been used as natural insecticides and repellents — a use reflected in the European folk tradition of laying wormwood amongst stored clothing and grain to repel moths and other insects.
 
== Traditional medicinal uses ==
 
''A. scoparia'' has been used as a medicinal plant in China since at least the [[Eastern Han dynasty]] (25–220 AD), where it is documented in the ''[[Shennong Bencao Jing]]'' ({{lang|zh|神農本草經}}), the earliest Chinese pharmacopoeia. Under the name ''Yinchen'', it has been employed for liver-protective, bile-stimulating ([[cholagogue]]), and [[diuretic]] purposes for nearly two millennia.<ref name="ding2021"/> The plant is well known as an ingredient of diuretic and detoxifying medicines.<ref name="florachina"/>
 
Traditional indications have included [[jaundice]] (described in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] as dampness–heat patterns in the liver and gallbladder), [[hepatitis]] and other disorders of the liver and gallbladder including [[cholecystitis]], dyspepsia, gastritis, fever, pain, pruritus, sores, expulsion of intestinal parasites, and respiratory conditions including [[asthma]].<ref name="ding2021"/><ref name="sharifirad2022">{{cite journal |last1=Sharifi-Rad |first1=Javad |year=2022 |title=Artemisia spp.: An Update on Its Chemical Composition, Pharmacological and Toxicological Profiles |journal=Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity |volume=2022 |article-number=5628601 |doi=10.1155/2022/5628601 |doi-access=free |pmid=36105486 |pmc=9467740}}</ref> It has an antibacterial action, inhibiting the growth of ''[[Staphylococcus aureus]]'', streptococci, ''[[Shigella|Bacillus dysenteriae]]'', ''[[Salmonella|B. typhi]]'', ''[[Bacillus subtilis|B. subtilis]]'', pneumococci, ''[[Corynebacterium diphtheriae|C. diphtheriae]]'', and mycobacteria.<ref name="yeung1985">{{cite book |last=Yeung |first=Him-Che |year=1985 |title=Handbook of Chinese Herbs and Formulas |publisher=Institute of Chinese Medicine |location=Los Angeles}}</ref>
 
A classical TCM prescription for jaundice combined ''A. scoparia'' with ''[[Gardenia jasminoides]]'' J. Ellis and rhubarb (''[[Rheum rhabarbarum]]'' L.), a formulation known as '''Yin-Chen-Hao decoction''' ({{lang|zh|茵陳蒿湯}}, YCHD), which continues to be studied pharmacologically.<ref name="ding2021"/> Beyond China, the plant has been used in the folk medicine traditions of Central Asia, Korea, Japan, India, and Pakistan.
 
== Pharmacology ==
 
Modern pharmacological research has demonstrated that ''A. scoparia'' possesses a broad spectrum of bioactivities. The most extensively studied are its effects on the liver and gallbladder, its anti-inflammatory activity, and its effects on metabolic disease. The preponderance of evidence to date derives from ''[[in vitro]]'' cell culture experiments and animal models; human clinical trial data remain limited.<ref name="ding2021"/><ref name="boudreau2022">{{cite journal |last1=Boudreau |first1=Adeline |last2=Richard |first2=Allison J. |last3=Harvey |first3=Innocence |last4=Stephens |first4=Jacqueline M. |year=2022 |title=Artemisia scoparia and Metabolic Health: Untapped Potential of an Ancient Remedy for Modern Use |journal=Frontiers in Endocrinology |volume=12 |article-number=727061 |doi=10.3389/fendo.2021.727061 |doi-access=free |pmc=8861327 |pmid=35211087}}</ref>
 
=== Effects on the liver and gallbladder ===
 
The liver-protective properties of ''A. scoparia'' are among its best-characterised activities and provide scientific support for its long traditional use in liver and biliary disease. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that plant extracts protect against liver damage induced by [[carbon tetrachloride]] (CCl₄) and [[paracetamol|acetaminophen]] in animal models.<ref name="gilani1993">{{cite journal |last1=Gilani |first1=A.H. |last2=Janbaz |first2=K.H. |year=1993 |title=Protective effect of Artemisia scoparia extract against acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity |journal=General Pharmacology |volume=24 |issue=6 |pages=1455–1458 |doi=10.1016/0306-3623(93)90434-Y |pmid=8270157}}</ref>
 
''Artemisiae Scopariae'' Herba (ASH) is described as the most commonly used [[traditional Chinese medicine]] herbal preparation for chronic liver diseases, especially [[cholestasis|cholestatic liver diseases]].<ref name="zhu2020"/> Clinical evidence summarised in peer-reviewed literature has indicated that ASH-based TCM prescriptions may offer therapeutic benefit in cholestasis.<ref name="zhu2020"/>
 
The principal liver-protective mechanisms involve several bioactive constituents working in different ways:
 
* '''[[Scoparone]]''' (6,7-dimethoxycoumarin) exerts anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic effects. It has shown activity in animal models of acute liver injury, alcohol-induced liver damage, [[non-alcoholic fatty liver disease]] (NAFLD), and hepatic fibrosis. Key mechanisms include inhibition of the [[NF-κB]] inflammatory signalling pathway and modulation of bile acid transporters. Scoparone is the principal active component of the classical TCM formulations Yin-Chen-Hao decoction (YCHD) and Yinzhihuang decoction (YZHD).<ref name="scoparonereview">{{cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Y. |last2=Liu |first2=W. |last3=Zhou |first3=X. |year=2021 |title=Scoparone as a therapeutic drug in liver diseases: Pharmacology, pharmacokinetics and molecular mechanisms of action |journal=Pharmacology & Therapeutics |volume=220 |issue=3 |pages=477–484 |doi=10.1016/j.pharmthera.2020.107659 |pmid=33217469}}</ref><ref name="aschema"/>
* '''Capillarisin''' contributes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.<ref name="ding2021"/>
* '''Chlorogenic acid''' and its isomers confer further antioxidant and anti-inflammatory protection.<ref name="zhu2020"/>
* '''β-Sitosterol''' isolated from the plant has been studied in liver fibrosis models.<ref name="ding2021"/>
 
A 2026 study published in ''[[Frontiers in Pharmacology]]'' reported that ''A. scoparia'' extract inhibits oxidative stress and [[ferroptosis]] in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH) through AGE-RAGE and JAK1-STAT3 signalling pathways.<ref name="frontiers2026">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Linlin |last2=Miao |first2=Yu |last3=Wang |first3=Hailong |last4=Hasimu |first4=Hamulati |last5=Ji |first5=Tengfei |last6=Huang |first6=Hua |last7=Du |first7=Guanhua |last8=Aisa |first8=Haji Akber |last9=Xin |first9=Xuelei |year=2026 |title=Artemisia scoparia extract inhibits oxidative stress and ferroptosis to ameliorate MASH through AGE-RAGE and JAK1-STAT3 signaling |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |volume=17 |article-number=1792221 |doi=10.3389/fphar.2026.1792221 |doi-access=free |pmid=42064791 |pmc=13125038 }}</ref>
 
=== Anti-inflammatory activity ===
 
Comprehensive anti-inflammatory activity has been documented across multiple cell types and experimental settings. A study published in the journal ''[[Obesity (journal)|Obesity]]'' (Boudreau et al., 2020) demonstrated that an ethanolic extract of ''A. scoparia'' inhibits inflammatory responses in cultured [[adipocyte]]s, [[macrophage]]s, and pancreatic [[beta cell|β-cells]] through two distinct signalling pathways — the [[ERK]] kinase pathway and the [[NF-κB]] pathway.<ref name="boudreau2020">{{cite journal |last1=Boudreau |first1=Adeline |last2=Burke |first2=Susan J. |last3=Collier |first3=J. Jason |last4=Richard |first4=Allison J. |last5=Ribnicky |first5=David M. |last6=Stephens |first6=Jacqueline M. |year=2020 |title=Mechanisms of Artemisia scoparia's Anti-Inflammatory Activity in Cultured Adipocytes, Macrophages, and Pancreatic β-Cells |journal=Obesity |volume=28 |issue=9 |pages=1726–1735 |doi=10.1002/oby.22912 |pmid=32741148 |pmc=7483878 }}</ref> Scoparone has also been shown to inhibit the production of inflammatory mediators through suppression of NF-κB activation, and its immune-regulatory effects have been reviewed in the context of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases.<ref name="scoparoneimmuno">{{cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=F. |last2=Lin |first2=J. |last3=Huang |first3=X. |last4=Yang |first4=B. |last5=Lu |first5=W. |last6=Dai |first6=Z. |year=2025 |title=The immunoregulatory effects of scoparone on immune-mediated inflammatory diseases |journal=Frontiers in Immunology |volume=16 |article-number=1518886 |doi=10.3389/fimmu.2025.1518886 |doi-access=free |pmid=39958341 |pmc=11825328}}</ref>
 
=== Metabolic effects ===
 
An emerging body of peer-reviewed research has demonstrated potential for ''A. scoparia'' extracts in [[metabolic syndrome|metabolic disease]], particularly [[obesity]], [[insulin resistance]], and [[type 2 diabetes]], published principally in ''PLOS ONE'', ''Obesity'', ''Nutrition'', and ''Frontiers in Endocrinology''. A 2022 review in ''Frontiers in Endocrinology'' provides a comprehensive synthesis of these findings, concluding that the plant represents "untapped potential of an ancient remedy for modern use" in metabolic health, while noting that human clinical trials remain necessary to establish efficacy.<ref name="boudreau2022"/>
 
=== Antimicrobial activity ===
 
Essential oils of ''A. scoparia'' have demonstrated antimicrobial activity against bacterial and fungal pathogens ''in vitro''.<ref name="cha2005">{{cite journal |last1=Cha |first1=J.-D. |last2=Jeong |first2=M.-R. |last3=Jeong |first3=S.-I. |year=2005 |title=Chemical composition and antimicrobial activity of the essential oils of ''Artemisia scoparia'' and ''A. capillaris'' |journal=Planta Medica |volume=71 |issue=2 |pages=186–190 |doi=10.1055/s-2005-837790 |pmid=15729626 |bibcode=2005PlMed..71..186C }}</ref> Scoparone additionally exhibits antibacterial, antifungal, antiparasitic, and antiviral activity in laboratory studies.<ref name="zhu2020"/>
 
== Safety and toxicology ==
 
The pollen of ''A. scoparia'' is allergenic and has been identified as a cause of [[allergic rhinitis]] in sensitised individuals in regions where the plant is prevalent. Pollen allergens have been isolated and characterised.<ref name="jaggi1987"/> Although we have seen no specific reports for this species, many members of this genus contain potentially allergenic sesquiterpene lactones that can cause skin reactions.<ref name="temperate"/>
 
Comprehensive long-term ''in vivo'' toxicity data and formal clinical safety evaluations of ''A. scoparia'' extracts in humans are lacking. Reviewers have noted that comprehensive evaluation of long-term toxicity and clinical efficacy "require further in-depth research" before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding therapeutic use in human disease.<ref name="ding2021"/>
